t: COPD: definition and the two subtypes
q: what is COPD
what is the difference between chronic bronchitis and emphysema
what are blue bloaters and pink puffers
x: COPD is persistent airflow blockage plus breathing symptoms, caused by breathing in smoke or other particles. It is an umbrella over two subtypes. Chronic bronchitis is defined by symptoms: a cough with sputum for at least 3 months a year for 2 years in a row; the airways narrow and plug with mucus (the blue bloater, with cyanosis and swelling). Emphysema is defined by damage: the air sacs are destroyed and permanently enlarged, and the lung loses the elastic recoil that holds airways open (the pink puffer: thin, pursed lips, barrel chest). Diffusing capacity is low in emphysema and normal in chronic bronchitis. Chronic bronchitis without any blockage on spirometry is not COPD.

q: how is COPD diagnosed
what ratio confirms COPD
how is COPD different from asthma on spirometry
x: Spirometry before and after a bronchodilator is required. A ratio of the 1-second volume to forced vital capacity below 0.70 after the bronchodilator confirms COPD. An improvement under 12% means the blockage is irreversible, which points to COPD rather than asthma. A normal ratio with a low forced vital capacity suggests restriction instead, confirmed with total lung capacity.

q: how do you grade COPD severity
what is GOLD 3
x: Once the ratio is below 0.70, the grade comes from the post-bronchodilator 1-second volume as a percent of predicted. Grade 1 (mild) is 80% or more, grade 2 (moderate) is 50% to 79%, grade 3 (severe) is 30% to 49%, and grade 4 (very severe) is below 30%.

t: COPD groups: A, B, C, D and E
q: how do I assign a COPD group
what is group E
what is high exacerbation risk
x: Symptoms times risk gives the group. Symptoms are fewer if the assessment test is under 10 or the dyspnea grade is 0 to 1, and more if 10 or higher or grade 2 or more. Risk is high with 2 or more moderate exacerbations or 1 that needed hospitalization in the past year. The 2020 scheme has four groups: A (few symptoms, low risk), B (more symptoms, low risk), C (few symptoms, high risk), D (more symptoms, high risk). The current scheme has three: A, B, and E, where E is any high-risk patient. The group sets the first medicines: A gets one bronchodilator; B and E get a long-acting beta agonist plus a long-acting antimuscarinic, with an inhaled steroid considered in E when blood eosinophils are 300 or more.

q: how do you calculate the BODE index
what does the BODE index predict
x: The BODE index adds points for body mass index (21 or less scores 1), airflow (1-second volume: 65% or more 0, 50 to 64 1, 36 to 49 2, 35 or less 3), dyspnea grade (0 to 1 scores 0, 2 scores 1, 3 scores 2, 4 scores 3) and 6-minute walk distance (350 meters or more 0, 150 to 249 2, 149 or less 3). Total 0 to 2 predicts about 80% 4-year survival, 3 to 4 about 67%, 5 to 6 about 57%, and 7 to 10 about 18%.

q: what are the side effects of COPD inhalers
why is an inhaled steroid not used alone in COPD
x: Long-acting beta agonists can cause fast heart rate and arrhythmias, and can worsen atrial fibrillation. Long-acting antimuscarinics (like tiotropium) are poorly absorbed, so the main side effect is dry mouth. An inhaled corticosteroid is never used alone in COPD; it is always combined with a long-acting beta agonist, and it raises the risk of pneumonia. Oral steroids are for exacerbations only. Albuterol is the rescue inhaler for every patient, but too much carries heart and mood side effects.

q: when does someone with COPD need oxygen
does oxygen help COPD patients live longer
x: Oxygen is given when arterial oxygen is under 55 mmHg or saturation is below 88%. For severe low oxygen at rest it lowers the risk of death and improves quality of life. Saturation 88% or less at rest qualifies for oxygen more than 15 hours a day; 89% to 93% at rest does not; 88% or less only with exertion qualifies for oxygen during exertion; a drop only at night should lead to an evaluation for sleep apnea.

q: when do COPD exacerbations need antibiotics
when is a COPD exacerbation admitted
what helps hypercapnic respiratory failure in COPD
x: An exacerbation is a worsening of breathlessness, cough or sputum over 14 days or less, and more than 80% are treated at home. Treatment is bronchodilators, steroids and oxygen if needed; antibiotics are added when breathlessness comes with more and more purulent sputum (doxycycline, a macrolide, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole or amoxicillin-clavulanate; levofloxacin if Pseudomonas is a worry). Admission is for marked symptoms despite treatment, new edema, arrhythmia, need for noninvasive ventilation, big comorbidities or no home support. Noninvasive ventilation helps when carbon dioxide is retained and lowers intubation and death.

q: why not a dry powder inhaler in the elderly
how does COPD care change after 65
x: At 65 and older the fixed 0.70 ratio may overdiagnose, so clinical judgment matters. Priorities shift to function, quality of life, other illnesses and goals of care. Arthritis, tremor, memory problems or weak inspiratory flow make dry powder inhalers hard to use, so a metered-dose inhaler with a spacer, a soft mist inhaler or a nebulizer is better. Watch for too many drugs, anticholinergic burden, heart effects of beta agonists, and pneumonia and fracture risk from inhaled steroids. Older adults are referred to rehabilitation less often, so refer them on purpose, and bring in palliative care early.

q: when should I test for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency
what does alpha-1 emphysema look like
x: This inherited deficiency (about 3 or 4 per 10,000) causes panlobular emphysema in the lower lobes. Think of it when emphysema appears at 45 or younger, in a nonsmoker or minimal smoker, mostly at the lung bases, or with a family history. Smoking emphysema is instead centrilobular and mostly in the upper lobes. The diagnosis is a low enzyme level (below 11 micromol/L) with a severely deficient genotype.
